56:2.text: (For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)

provenance.other: “our warfare” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 10:4. The noun itself is rare — “warfare” occurs in exactly five KJV verses — and in the possessive it is Paul's alone. “strong holds” is commoner (nineteen KJV verses), so it carries nothing by itself; what is worth noting is that Alma 56 uses both of 2 Corinthians 10:4's two distinctive nouns, at 56:2 and again at 56:21 ('we were not desirous to make an attack upon them in their strong holds').
provenance.significance: Helaman's letter opens in the register of a Pauline epistle — a named addressee, 'my dearly beloved brother', the pairing 'as well in the Lord as in the tribulations of our warfare' — and the phrase it reaches for is from the one Pauline passage that insists the warfare in question is not the kind fought with weapons. 2 Corinthians 10:3-4 says 'though we walk in the flesh, we do not war after the flesh: for the weapons of our warfare are not carnal'. Alma 56 then spends fifty-five verses on weapons that emphatically are carnal, and ends by saying that the young men who carried them 'fought as if with the strength of God' and that not one of them fell. The letter borrows Paul's phrase for a spiritual campaign and applies it to an actual one, and the chapter's own explanation of the outcome — strength that is not the soldiers' own — is Paul's 'mighty through God' arriving by a different road.

56:2.note: 'My dearly beloved brother, Moroni, as well in the Lord as in the tribulations of our warfare.' 'Our warfare' is a KJV singleton and it belongs to 2 Corinthians 10:4; the epistolary frame around it is Pauline in shape, and 'strong holds', the other distinctive noun of that verse, returns at 56:21. Recorded at moderate because a first-person plural possessive on a common noun is easy to generate independently, and because the two words are nineteen verses apart in the Book of Mormon rather than adjacent as they are in Paul.
56:2.whyNot: Two words, one of them a pronoun. 'Warfare' is ordinary English and 'our warfare' would be produced by anyone writing a war letter in the first person plural; the KJV singleton may be an accident of how seldom the KJV uses the noun at all.

56:37.text: And Asahel pursued after Abner; and in going he turned not to the right hand nor to the left from following Abner.

provenance.other: “turned not to the right hand” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 2:19. The fuller formula “to the right hand nor to the left” occurs in exactly five KJV verses, and the other four are all about conduct rather than pursuit: two are requests to pass peaceably through a country (Numbers 20:17, Deuteronomy 2:27), one is obedience to a judicial sentence (Deuteronomy 17:11), one is Proverbs 4:27 on moral straightness, and 2 Chronicles 34:2 is Josiah's walk. 2 Samuel 2:19 is the only KJV verse in which the phrase describes a man chasing another man.
provenance.significance: The recovered context is the whole point and it is grim. Asahel's refusal to turn to the right hand or the left is not praised in 2 Samuel 2; it is the reason he dies. Abner turns and warns him twice — 'turn thee aside to thy right hand or to thy left' (2:21), 'wherefore should I smite thee to the ground?' (2:22) — and Asahel will not, and Abner kills him with the hinder end of the spear. Alma 56:37 gives the phrase to the Lamanite army pursuing Helaman, and gives it in the same posture: the pursuer who will not deviate, running down a smaller force, with a second army closing behind. Helaman even names the danger Abner named — 'it was their intent to slay us before Antipus should overtake them, and this that they might not be surrounded by our people' — and the outcome is the one 2 Samuel 2 predicts for the man who does not turn aside. At 56:40 the phrase is turned around and applied to Helaman himself, so both parties in the chase are Asahel, and neither can afford to be.

56:37.note: 'They did not turn to the right nor to the left, but pursued their march in a straight course after us.' The KJV's one pursuit-verse using this formula, and the Book of Mormon has it in a pursuit. The one departure is the dropped noun: every KJV instance reads 'right hand', and Alma 56:37 and 56:40 both read 'right' alone, which is the phrase compressed rather than a different phrase. Note that 56:40 uses it twice more in three lines, once of the Lamanites and once of Helaman — a doubling that reads as a writer working a borrowed formula rather than reaching for an idiom of his own.

56:46.text: Take counsel together, and it shall come to nought; speak the word, and it shall not stand: for God is with us.

provenance.other: “God is with us” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 8:10 — the translation of Immanuel worked into the oracle itself. Matthew 1:23 has the interpretation without the verb ('Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us'), so the finite clause the Book of Mormon uses is Isaiah's and not the Gospel's.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 8:9-10 is a war oracle addressed to armies, and the sons of the stripling warriors answer their commander with its last clause. Recover the context and the whole of what Helaman's young men are claiming becomes visible: 'Associate yourselves, O ye people, and ye shall be broken in pieces … Take counsel together, and it shall come to nought; speak the word, and it shall not stand: for God is with us.' That is a promise that an enemy's confederacy and an enemy's plan will fail, which is exactly the news of Alma 56 — Ammoron's orders at 56:18 and 56:20 keep his armies from attacking, the pursuit at 56:37 is a plan that comes to nought, and the chapter closes with the pursuers surrendering. The young men say four words and the source supplies the argument for them. Note also that the KJV's sole occurrence of the clause sits between the two Immanuel verses (Isaiah 7:14, 8:8), so the phrase these sons of a converted people use of themselves is the name given to a promised child.

56:46.note: 'Father, behold, our God is with us, and he will not suffer that we shall fall.' A KJV singleton, and the one place in the Bible where the clause is a finite sentence rather than a gloss on a name. The interpolated possessive ('our God is with us') is the Book of Mormon making the clause the speakers' own, and it fits the chapter's insistence that this faith was taught to them and not inherited from the fathers, who had buried their weapons. The second half of the young men's answer, 'he will not suffer that we shall fall', is then cashed out at 56:56, where not one of them has fallen.

56:47.text: Jesus answered and said unto them, Verily I say unto you, If ye have faith, and doubt not, ye shall not only do this which is done to the fig tree, but also if ye shall say unto this mountain, Be thou removed, and be thou cast into the sea; it shall be done.

provenance.other: “doubt not” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 21:21. The word appears in thirteen KJV verses altogether, but in nine of them it is the adverbial 'no doubt' or the noun; the only two places where doubting is negated as a condition of a promise are Matthew 21:21 and its Markan double, Mark 11:23's 'shall not doubt in his heart, but shall believe'.
provenance.significance: The mothers' teaching is given in the grammar of the KJV's mountain-moving saying: a negated doubt as the condition, and a guaranteed outcome as the apodosis. What the Book of Mormon changes is who holds the condition. In Matthew the promise is to the one who does not doubt; in Alma 56:47-48 the young men do not doubt because their mothers did not, and the sentence they actually say is about someone else's certainty — 'we do not doubt our mothers knew it'. That is a displacement worth naming: the faith that moves the mountain has been made hereditary and second-hand, and the chapter treats that as a strength rather than a defect.
provenance.alternative: James 1:6's 'ask in faith, nothing wavering' is the same doctrine in different words and could stand behind the sentiment without any of Matthew's wording.

56:47.note: 'They had been taught by their mothers, that if they did not doubt, that God would deliver them.' The conditional is the KJV's and so is the negated verb, though the Book of Mormon inflects it ('did not doubt', 'do not doubt') rather than reproducing Matthew's imperative form 'doubt not'. Filed as an echo, not an allusion, because the only shared content word is 'doubt' and the shape of the sentence is doing most of the work.
56:47.whyNot: One content word. Doubt is the natural antonym for the faith the passage is about, and a writer describing a taught confidence would arrive at the negation without any source. The rarity count is real but it measures the KJV's vocabulary, not this verse's dependence.

56:56.text: Then said she, I pray thee, let the king remember the LORD thy God, that thou wouldest not suffer the revengers of blood to destroy any more, lest they destroy my son. And he said, As the LORD liveth, there shall not one hair of thy son fall to the earth.

provenance.other: “one hair of thy son” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 14:11, and “not one hair” in exactly two, that verse and 1 Samuel 14:45. The verb phrase “fall to the earth” occurs in exactly three KJV verses; taking earth and ground together, the KJV's fixed formula 'there shall not one hair … fall to the earth/ground' occurs at 1 Samuel 14:45, 2 Samuel 14:11 and 1 Kings 1:52 and nowhere else. Alma 56:56 has the formula with 'earth', which is 2 Samuel 14:11's and 1 Kings 1:52's word, and with 'soul' substituted for 'hair'.
provenance.significance: All three KJV verses carrying this formula are guarantees that a particular young man under sentence of death will be spared: Jonathan, whom the people rescue from his father's oath after he alone attacked a garrison and wrought a great salvation; the widow of Tekoah's surviving son, spared from the avengers of blood; and Adonijah, spared on condition. Two of the three are pleas made by a parent or on a son's behalf, and 2 Samuel 14:11 is the mother's. Alma 56:56 reports the outcome of a battle fought by two thousand sons whose commander calls them his own and whose mothers' faith is the chapter's stated cause of their survival, and it reports it in the formula the KJV reserves for a threatened son who is spared. 1 Samuel 14:45 sharpens it further: Jonathan is the KJV's one young man who attacks a superior garrison on the conviction that 'there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few', which is the doctrine Helaman's letter exists to demonstrate.

56:56.note: 'There had not one soul of them fallen to the earth.' The KJV has one way of saying that a young man in danger will not be lost, and this is it, with 'soul' for 'hair' because two thousand men and not one man is the quantity in view. The substitution is the Book of Mormon's, and it is not a weakening: 'not one hair' is a figure for total preservation and 'not one soul' makes the same claim literally. The 1830 reading is unchanged here, so nothing in the transmission is doing the work.

56:56.text: And they said unto Moses, Thy servants have taken the sum of the men of war which are under our charge, and there lacketh not one man of us.

provenance.other: “there lacketh not one man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and so does “taken the sum of the men of war”; both are Numbers 31:49. There is no verbal contact with Alma 56:55-56 at all — the Book of Mormon numbers rather than takes the sum, and its men are souls rather than men — so the count is recorded to show that the scene is a KJV singleton, not to claim the wording.
provenance.significance: This catalogue declined Numbers 31:49 once already, at Alma 49:23, on the ground that not one word is shared and the Book of Mormon's 'not a single soul' is in no KJV verse. That reasoning was right there and it does not reach here, because Alma 56:55 supplies what 49:23 lacked: the muster itself. Numbers 31:48-49 is a scene, not a phrase — subordinate officers come to the commander after a battle, report that they have counted the men under their charge, and report that none is missing — and Alma 56:55-56 is that scene entire, with the added detail that Helaman counts 'fearing lest there were many of them slain' and that the report reaches Moroni as a letter, which is the only form a subordinate's post-battle census can take at this distance. The KJV has exactly one such scene. That the Book of Mormon reproduces it without reproducing a word of it is the finding.

56:56.note: 'I numbered those young men which had fought with me, fearing lest there were many of them slain. But behold, to my great joy, there had not one soul of them fallen to the earth.' Filed as figural under CONVENTIONS §2 because the link is at the level of the scene and there is no shared wording to test; kjvSpecific is 'no' for the same reason, and no claim about the King James English is being made. The verbal case at this verse is carried by the separate row on 2 Samuel 14:11. Compare the exclusion at Alma 49:23, which sent the same source away for want of exactly what 56:55 provides.
56:56.whyNot: Zero verbal contact, and a commander counting his men after a battle is a natural thing to narrate. If Numbers 31:49 is the only KJV instance, that may say more about how rarely the KJV narrates a muster than about where Alma 56:55 came from — and a reader who applied the Alma 49:23 reasoning consistently would decline this row too.
